source: KOMBINE (2025/26 preprint) Table 10: blending scores per model
finding: The 43.4% valid-generic-space average hides a huge spread. The best models pass the generic-space utility check on 83.3% of blend items, the worst on 6.7%. So the abstraction bottleneck is model-dependent, not fixed.
numbers: Blend utility (valid generic space), % of max: gpt-5.6-sol 83.3, gemini-3.1-pro 83.3, gpt-6-astra 73.3, gemini-3.7-flash 70.0, claude-fable-5 60.0, claude-opus-4.6 56.7, claude-sonnet-5 40.0, deepseek-r1 43.3, deepseek-chat 40.0, gpt-4o-mini 16.7, phi-4 6.7. Humans 12.8. Scores move in steps of 3.33, which implies about 30 blend items per model (inferred, not stated).
limits: One pass per item per model at T=0.9, no scaffold arm, so it cannot say whether a scaffold lifts the low scorers. Reasoning variants do not clearly win: deepseek-r1 blend composite 30.4 vs deepseek-chat 28.1 vs deepseek-v3 20.1; gemini-2.5-pro 26.9 vs gemini-2.5-flash 18.8. LLM-judged.
agent_relevance: Gap 2: a scaffold has most to gain on mid and low models. Our agent should log generic-space validity separately from blend coherence, since the first is where the loss sits.

source: KOMBINE appendix: judge reliability and human check
finding: Judge reliability is only fair to good. One author, not independent raters, checked 60 items. Agreement is 66% with the panel majority and 75% where all three judges agree.
numbers: ICC(2,3) for the 3-judge panel on 1,023 artifacts: blend semantic integration 0.67 (good), blend utility G(g) 0.67 (good), analogy integration 0.56 (fair), analogy utility 0.55 (fair), blend utility V(c) 0.48 (fair). Human subsample: 60 items (30 analogy, 30 blend), 150 dimension judgments, 66% agreement with majority; n=96 unanimous judgments, 75%. Ranking on the unanimous-only subsample: Spearman 0.945, Pearson 0.941 (n=21 models); top eight only: Spearman 0.79, Pearson 0.86.
limits: A single human rater who is an author. No harder-slice or disagreement-slice analysis. 75% on unanimous items implies a 25% error floor even on the easy slice. Rankings are robust, absolute rates less so.
agent_relevance: Gap 9: do not trust absolute blend-validity rates from an LLM judge; use rank order only. For our agent, a model-run validity check disagrees with a human about 25-34% of the time, so it cannot be the only gate.

source: KOMBINE: limitations section
finding: The paper names its own limits: human sample is average Prolific adults, no domain experts, and analogy and blending overlap (structure mapping is part of building a blend). No test of any prompt or scaffold that targets the generic-space step.
numbers: Humans N=75; temperature 0.9 with top-p and top-k off; 35 LLMs.
limits: Absence of a scaffold test is itself the finding for Gap 1 and Gap 2 in this paper.
agent_relevance: Gap 1/2 stay open for blends proper: no reasoning-accuracy test with an explicit generic-space step exists in this source.

source: Peng et al. (2025) CreativeMashup: fusion vs replacement, read from the text
finding: For the identification task, fusion mashups were identified more precisely than replacement mashups in 9 of 11 models, and people showed the same pattern. The authors explain it: fusion shows readable traits of both objects, replacement shows mostly one.
numbers: 9 of 11 models higher precision on fusion (Fig. 5). Exact per-type percentages are only in a figure and were not extractable. Overall: GPT-4o identification P 75.67 R 85.00; average people P 53.42 R 70.33.
limits: Internal inconsistency: the Figure 5 caption says precision is 'consistently higher for replacement-based' while the body text says higher for fusion. The text, the explanation and the 'mirroring human performance' claim all say fusion, so the caption looks like a typo, but it is unresolved. Images, not text. Identification of existing mashups, not generation of blends.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: partly closed. The split is about how readable the blend is, not about blend quality, and it was measured on images. No text-only per-type rates exist in this source.

source: Sato (2025) Triggering hallucinations in LLMs: prompt-induced hallucination (HIP, HQP)
finding: Asking a model to fuse two incompatible domains (periodic table plus tarot) gave higher judged hallucination than asking it to compare the same two topics. A logically sound fusion (aperiodic tilings plus crafts) scored lower than the comparison prompt.
numbers: Prompts matched at 29-30 tokens, two sentences. Six models, 3 independent responses each, each scored 5 times by a GPT-o3 judge on a 0-10 scale (n=15 per model for HIPc; n=10 per condition in Fig. 2). One-tailed Welch t-tests; HIPn lower than HIPc, p<0.01. Order of HIPc score: DeepSeek-R1 > DeepSeek > GPT-4o ~ GPT-o3 ~ Gemini2.0Flash > Gemini2.5Pro (score 2 treated as baseline). DeepSeek-R1 above DeepSeek, p about 0.048.
quote: Semantic fusion without conceptual grounding emerges as a core risk factor of hallucination.
limits: One fused prompt pair and one logical pair; replicates are repeated scoring of 3 responses, not independent prompts. Single LLM judge, same family as one tested model. Author states the design was made in dialogue with an LLM. No human grading. The compared prompts also differ in task (build a theory vs compare), so fusion is confounded with request type.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: the closest measured data on 'blend without grounding'. Direction fits the idea that a check on whether the blend is grounded should cut ungrounded output, but this paper did not test a fix.

source: Xu et al. (2026) Beyond Pixels: schema-driven visual metaphor transfer, human ablation
finding: The only direct ablation of an explicit generic-space step that was found. The pipeline extracts a schema with a generic space (relational invariant), transfers it, generates, then diagnoses. Removing the blending-theory schema description, while keeping multi-stage prompting and iteration, lowered human ratings on the conceptual scales.
numbers: Human study, 100 participants (age 14-55, 45 male, 55 female), 45 images per method per person, 5-point scales. Ablation user study means (MR / MI / VA / VI / VQ): Direct prompt 3.62/2.75/2.96/3.75/3.65; Strong prompt (one-shot CBT prompt) 3.97/3.69/3.77/3.89/4.09; w/o CBT description 3.88/3.66/3.68/4.04/4.12; w/o transfer agent 4.01/3.71/3.83/4.33/4.25; w/o diagnostic agent 4.26/4.05/3.98/4.61/4.48; full 4.47/4.56/4.51/4.74/4.76. Versus commercial generators the full system was preferred in 64.44% (GPT-Image) and 67.11% (Banana-pro) of pairs, 72.89% vs Midjourney, 76.22% vs BAGEL. Cost: about 8.3k tokens and 4 min 11 s per sample; 126 metaphors; mean calls Perception 1.14, Transfer 1.25, Generation 2.19, Diagnostic 2.19.
limits: Image metaphors, not reasoning. Not equal compute: the full system uses iteration and several agents, and the direct-prompt arm has no iteration. No SDs or tests in the extracted table. The VLM-judge table (Table 1) extracted with garbled row labels and was not used. Authors designed the metric and the baselines. The Strong prompt arm is the fairest control: the full system still gains 0.50 MR, 0.87 MI, 0.74 VA over it.
agent_relevance: Gap 1/8: evidence that a structured schema with an explicit invariant plus a check beats a single strong prompt on a creative transfer task, in human ratings. It does not show gain on accuracy-style reasoning. The diagnostic (check) agent adds a further 0.2 to 0.5 on the conceptual scales.

source: Zheng et al. (2024) Take a Step Back: abstraction before reasoning
finding: A separate abstraction step (derive the principle or higher-level question first, then reason) beats zero-shot chain of thought on knowledge-heavy tasks with PaLM-2L, and by a smaller margin with GPT-4. This is the nearest tested analogue of a generic-space step, but it abstracts one input; it does not find structure shared by two inputs.
numbers: MMLU Physics / Chemistry: PaLM-2L 66.4/70.9; +CoT 65.0/75.3; +Step-Back 73.2/81.8. GPT-4 69.4/80.9; +CoT 82.9/85.3; +Step-Back 84.5/85.6 (SD 1.2 and 1.4; gain over CoT 1.6 and 0.3 points, about one SD or less). TimeQA PaLM-2L +CoT 40.8 vs +Step-Back 66.0 (68.7 with RAG). MuSiQue +CoT 38.7 vs +Step-Back 42.6; StrategyQA 83.6 vs 82.7 (no gain). Error analysis: Step-Back fixes up to about 40% of base-model errors and adds at most about 12% new errors; more than 90% of remaining errors are in the reasoning step, not the abstraction step.
limits: Two model calls, so not equal tokens against one-pass CoT; no compute-matched arm. Strong model (GPT-4) gain over CoT is within noise on MMLU. The abstraction is of one problem, not a cross-input generic space. Few-shot demonstrations for the step-back question are hand-written.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (indirect): abstraction scaffolds help a weaker model clearly and a strong model barely. Supports putting the generic-space step behind a gate for strong models and testing it at equal tokens.

source: Yasunaga et al. (2024) Large language models as analogical reasoners (ICLR)
finding: Having the model recall its own related problems and then solve outperforms zero-shot and few-shot CoT on GSM8K, MATH, Codeforces and BIG-Bench tasks. The authors report the benefit is larger for larger models and that retrieved examples work better for small models.
numbers: Tables 1 and 2 were read but the row labels extracted garbled, so per-cell numbers are not used here. Text claims only: gains over 0-shot CoT and manual few-shot CoT across GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, PaLM2, text-davinci-003; self-generated knowledge plus exemplars adds more on Codeforces.
limits: Numbers not safely extracted. Analogy to related problems, not a blend. No compute-matched control read.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 (indirect): scaffolds that make the model produce related structure first do help, mostly for larger models. Same direction as d07.

source: de Vega, Urrutia and Riffo (2007) Canceling updating in the comprehension of counterfactuals embedded in narratives. Memory & Cognition 35(6)
finding: Counterfactual comprehension (a mental-space case) holds two readings at once at first: the as-if 'p and q' scenario and the 'not-p, not-q' real situation. The as-if reading fades after a further clause. This gives a time course for two spaces but does not test the order composition, completion, elaboration.
numbers: Exp 1 self-paced reading: 60 students (6 dismissed). Interaction context x final situation F1(1,53)=8.60, p=.005; F2(1,47)=5.66. Old-situation clauses read faster after counterfactuals [t1(53)=2.87, p=.006]; new-situation clauses faster after factuals [t1(53)=4.95, p<.0001]. Coherence judgment: interaction F1(1,53)=6.12, p=.02; counterfactual-old responses 142 ms slower. Exp 2 probe recognition (N=40; 15% probe errors dropped): old information more accessible after counterfactuals, new equally accessible; target position F1(1,35)=48.73, p<.0001. Exp 3 (77 recruited, 16 dismissed, 61 analysed): after extra clauses the final probe was recognised faster in factual than counterfactual stories [t1(60)=3.25, p=.002]; errors 19% initial vs 13% final.
quote: counterfactual events are momentarily represented but are later suppressed
limits: Reading and probe times, students, one language. It does not mention the blend operation order. It supports a double representation whose as-if space is later suppressed, which fits a blend network, but also fits non-blending accounts (update cancelling). Attrition up to 20% in Exp 3.
agent_relevance: Gap 5: the primary paper does not contradict the operation order; it says nothing on that order. Treat blends as short-lived: an agent should not keep the as-if space alive after the question is settled.

source: Ferguson and Sanford (2008) Anomalies in real and counterfactual worlds: an eye-movement investigation. J Memory and Language 58(3), 609-626
finding: Three eye-tracking studies. Real-world violations are not neutralised by a counterfactual context: 'cats eat carrots' after 'if cats were vegetarians' still slows early reading, as much as a plain real-world violation. The authors conclude the reader checks each proposition against real-world knowledge just before building it into the counterfactual world. They support a dual, possibly two-stage process. The paper cites Fauconnier and Turner only as background for mental spaces and does not test blend operation order.
numbers: Exp 1: 36 Glasgow undergraduates, 24 items. Critical-region first-pass time F1(2,35)=5.2, p<.01; F2(2,23)=3.7, p=.03. RW-inconsistent longer than RW-consistent t1(35)=2.8, p<.05; CW-consistent longer than RW-consistent t1(35)=2.8, p<.05; CW-consistent vs RW-inconsistent ts<0.2 (no difference). Regression path time F1(2,35)=4.3, p=.02. Exp 2: 36 new participants (RW context primed to rule out priming). Exp 3: 36 participants, modal 'would' continuation; real-world effects last longer, into later measures.
quote: Even within a counterfactual context, participants appear to still automatically process information in terms of their real-world knowledge.
limits: Students, English, single sentences. Does not address composition, completion, elaboration. It shows the as-if space does not cleanly screen out real-world knowledge, closer to leaky projection than strict selective projection, but the authors do not frame it as a test of blending.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 closed: neither primary paper contradicts the order. Practical lesson: when an agent runs a blend, input-space facts leak in at once, so check the blend against real-world constraints before accepting it.

source: Jiang et al. (2025) Artificial Hivemind: open-ended homogeneity of language models (NeurIPS D&B)
finding: Open-ended output repeats across samples and across models. This is the general background for KOMBINE's blend homogeneity, and it holds with diversity decoding too.
numbers: INFINITY-CHAT: 26K real open-ended queries, 70+ models (25 detailed), 31,250 human annotations with 25 raters per item. Same-model repetition at temperature 1.0 and top-p 0.9: in 79% of cases average similarity between responses exceeds 0.8. Min-p decoding: 81% of response pairs still above 0.7 similarity, 61.2% above 0.8. Between-model average pairwise similarity 71% to 82%; DeepSeek-V3 vs qwen-max 0.82; DeepSeek-V3 vs gpt-4o 0.81.
limits: Not a blending study. Embedding similarity is a proxy for sameness of idea. No count of how many samples are needed to reach a new idea.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: blends are not special; more samples from the same model give the same answer. Escaping likely needs different frames or inputs, not more samples at the same prompt. Untested for blend prompts.

source: Lynn (2026) Conceptual blending in humans and language models. Frontiers in Psychology 17:1849083
finding: Conceptual analysis, no experiment. Claims that goals decide which features of the inputs are projected into a blend (selective projection driven by goal and affordances) and that LLMs use proxy goals from alignment and prompt framing. Illustrated by a toy vector-symbolic model in Python.
numbers: No sample, no measured results. Received 2026 Apr 7, accepted 2026 Jul 14.
limits: Theory only. A toy script is not a benchmark.
agent_relevance: Gap 8: gives a testable idea: name the goal before projecting. Our agent could add a goal line to the blend step and measure incoherent blends with a rule-based check, but nobody has.

source: Gomez-Ramirez and Turner (2026) Formal conceptual blending for Artificial Mathematical Intelligence (CogSci 2026 poster)
finding: Poster co-authored by Turner (a founder of the theory). Formalises a blend of two concepts along a generic space as partial cross-space mappings, selective projection and emergent models beyond the union of the inputs. Proposes a blend-aware fine-tuning loss L = L_task + lambda L_blend that scores each latent step against a valid transformation of the blended structure.
numbers: No experiment, no data on the poster.
limits: Proposal. Training-time idea, so outside our no-training constraint. The claim that LLM maths failures are failures of conceptual integration is untested.
agent_relevance: Gap 8/10: shows a formal, checkable notion of valid selective projection (a model of the blend must satisfy the axioms of the inputs where projected). A symbolic check like this is the nearest thing to an LLM-free validity test, in a maths setting only.

source: Searches for monk riddle solve rates (arXiv and three web searches this pass)
finding: NEGATIVE FINDING again. No study with a solve rate for the Buddhist monk riddle or its isomorphs, human or LLM, with or without a one-path hint. Nearest hit: NazoNazo (Mizumoto et al., 2509.14704), Japanese children's riddles as an insight benchmark. Seen only through a search summary. The 92% hint figure seen earlier is the Gick and Holyoak radiation-problem hint result, a different task.
numbers: NazoNazo as summarised: 38 models, 201 riddles; non-reasoning models 7.6%, reasoning models 17.6%, humans about 52.9% on a 120-item subset. Not verified in paper text.
limits: Search summary only. Duncker 1945 and Gick-Holyoak not opened. Absence in reachable sources.
agent_relevance: Gap 4 stays open. Do not cite any monk-riddle rate. NazoNazo (models fail to endorse their own correct candidates) is a better proxy test bed, but not a blending test.

source: Hilpert (2010) and Schmid on blending versus relevance theory for noun-noun compounds
finding: NOT OPENED, and the Hilpert 2010 title could not be matched in search at all. Closest item: Sabzevari, 'Conceptual blending, relevance and novel N+N-compounds', in Handl and Schmid (eds.) Windows to the Mind (2011), pp. 219-246 (title only). No failed replication and no controlled blending-versus-relevance-theory experiment turned up.
numbers: None.
limits: Title-level pointers only; publisher pages blocked or unmatched.
agent_relevance: Gap 8 stays open. Treat the blending-versus-relevance debate as theoretical argument with no head-to-head data.

source: Visual Conceptual Blending with large-scale language and vision models (arXiv 2106.14127)
finding: A language model describes a blend of two objects and a text-to-image model draws it. Human raters on Mechanical Turk preferred the large-model pipeline (CLIP-guided BigSleep, DeepDaze) over a GAN baseline (DF-GAN) on blend, description fit and interest questions; BigSleep was preferred over DeepDaze.
numbers: Pairwise tests, 6 questions x 3 model pairs x 20 text descriptions, 9 unique raters per item. Questions mapped to the unpacking, integration and general-quality principles. Language models beat ConceptNet on a simile dataset (per-cell values garbled and not used).
limits: Only 20 descriptions; simile dataset; no reasoning task.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: a computational-blending lineage exists (Divago, PopBlends, this one) but all measure human preference on images or ideas, none measure task accuracy.

source: Coverage note: 2021-2026 arXiv and Europe PMC papers using conceptual blending in a model setting
finding: Listing found: PopBlends 2111.04920, Visual Conceptual Blending 2106.14127, nonword-to-image diffusion 2411.03595, Sato 2505.10948 and 2505.00557, CreativeMashup 2504.13120, KOMBINE 2509.21043, metaphor layers 2507.10354, schema-driven visual metaphor 2602.01335, ISWS creative-AI report 2501.18542. Europe PMC adds Lynn 2026 and a 2026 quantum-cognition paper on meaning construction.
numbers: About 10 arXiv items and 2 PMC items. Human-rated or measured comparisons: PopBlends, Visual Conceptual Blending, CreativeMashup, KOMBINE, Beyond Pixels, and Sato (judge only).
limits: After web search ran out, only arXiv search, Europe PMC and Crossref were reached. Education and computational-creativity venues (ACL Anthology, ICCC) were not reached. Titles 2507.10354, 2411.03595, 2501.18542 were not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: partly closed. No measured prompt-versus-prompt reasoning comparison for blending turned up in 2024-2026.

source: Yang et al. (2025) Vibe Spaces for Creatively Connecting and Expressing Visual Concepts (arXiv 2512.14884)
finding: Image blending method that finds the shared 'vibe' attributes of two inputs first (a generic-space-like step), then blends. Humans rate its blends as more creative and coherent than diffusion morphing and GPT and Gemini image generators. The paper also measures how well an LLM judge matches humans: only partly.
numbers: 10 human raters, pairwise comparisons on Totally Looks Like and an architecture set. Human-human agreement on which method's blend is preferred: 63-77% (Totally Looks Like), 66-75% (architecture); Cohen's kappa only 0.15-0.33. LLM judge picks the human top-1 blend 35.7% (TLL) and 31.3% (architecture) against 25% chance; human top-2 match 55.1% and 51.8%.
quote: humans are more consistent with one another, and the LLM captures a partial but meaningful overlap with human preferences.
limits: Images, not text. Only 10 raters. Authors' own method. Low kappa shows blend quality is a noisy human judgment too. No matched no-step arm seen in the passages read.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: an LLM judge of blend quality agrees with humans only a little above chance on the single best blend; human kappa is itself low. Do not score blend validity with an LLM judge alone. Gap 1 (partial): finding the relevant shared attributes first is the idea that works here.

source: Evaluating Creative Short Story Generation in Humans and Large Language Models (arXiv 2411.02316)
finding: LLM judges agree with each other but not well with humans on human-versus-AI judgments. Used here as a reliability benchmark for LLM creativity judging.
numbers: Human expert creativity judgments ICC .62-.90 (good to excellent). LLM judges (Claude, Gemini, GPT-4) among themselves ICC .86-.94. Human vs AI judgments ICC .43 (fair).
quote: human vs AI judgments (ICC=.43, fair inter-rater agreement)
limits: Short stories, not blends. ICC not kappa.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: high agreement among LLM judges can hide poor agreement with people. KOMBINE's judge checks (unanimous-item agreement) need a human-graded hard slice before the 43.4% figure is trusted.

source: Sato (2025) The Way We Prompt: Conceptual Blending Meets LLMs (arXiv 2505.10948)
finding: A position-style paper that frames prompt-induced transitions and hallucinations as blending. Abstract, theory and outlook sections scanned: no measured comparison, no baseline arm, no p-values or percentages.
numbers: None found in the full text (about 25 KB).
limits: Keyword and section scan, not a line-by-line read. Quantitative claims sit in the earlier Sato paper 2505.00557 (see d05).
agent_relevance: Gaps 3 and 5: no evidence here that blend prompts add real novelty or that projection limits reduce incoherence.

source: Eppe et al. (2018) A computational framework for conceptual blending. Artificial Intelligence 256
finding: Generalising the inputs (finding the generic space) is treated as a search problem solved with answer set programming, plus optimality principles to prune blends. Only the record page and abstract were opened. Evaluation is a proof-of-concept in mathematics and music. No numeric result and no non-blending baseline are stated.
numbers: None.
quote: we demonstrate how our system invents novel concepts and theories in domains where creativity is crucial
limits: Abstract level. The full PDF download failed. Divago results (Pereira) were seen only as a table of contents (Boat-House, Horse-Bird, noun-noun).
agent_relevance: Gap 10: classical computational blending has demonstrations, not controlled results. Its useful idea is generic space as an explicit search step with a pruning rule, which can be tested in an LLM scaffold.

source: Chilton, Petridis and Agrawala (2019) VisiBlends: A Flexible Workflow for Visual Blends. CHI 2019 (press release)
finding: A structured workflow (pick concepts, find shared shape or context, blend) helps novices make visual blends far more often than unguided work. Seen only in a search summary of the university press release.
numbers: Press release: 96% success with the tool against 21% without; 10 times as many creative results. Sample size and design not verified.
limits: Press-release figures from a search summary; paper text not opened. Authors' own system and task.
agent_relevance: Gap 10: the one blending-versus-no-structure comparison found. A workflow that forces explicit property matching before combining has a large reported effect for people, unverified. Needs the paper before use.

source: Latent-space ideation (arXiv 2507.13874) and 100-participant diffusion blending study (arXiv 2506.23630), from search summaries
finding: NOT OPENED. Search summaries: the ideation paper reports modest gains in originality and fluency over an LLM discussion baseline, judged by GPT-4o. The 100-participant diffusion study finds no single blending method wins everywhere (consistent with K14).
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Snippet level only.
agent_relevance: Gap 3: context only. No source found that measures how many samples are needed to escape cross-model repeated blends.

source: Searches for an equal-token test of an explicit generic-space or blend step against chain of thought
finding: NEGATIVE FINDING for gaps 1, 2, 3, 5 and 9. Web searches and arXiv listings (arXiv API rate-limited after the first calls) found no study that gives an LLM an explicit generic-space step and compares it with chain of thought at equal tokens; none that tries to lift the KOMBINE valid-generic-space rate with a scaffold; none that tests 'what not to carry over' with a non-LLM judge; none that reruns the fusion-versus-replacement split on text-only blends.
numbers: None.
limits: Absence of evidence in reachable sources. OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar were also rate-limited.
agent_relevance: These gaps stay open and are experiments to run in our own harness. Nearest indirect support: d07 and d08 (abstraction or self-generated analogies before solving help).

source: Judge-reliability snippets: arXiv 2411.15560 (AUT judges), 2502.03253 (humans vs LLM creativity reasoning), 2406.12624 (Judging the Judges)
finding: NOT OPENED, snippet only. LLM judges of the Alternate Uses Task correlate with each other (average Spearman above 0.7). In factual QA, GPT-4 Turbo reaches Cohen's kappa 84 against humans (human-human 96); the authors warn percent agreement can hide score differences.
numbers: Spearman >0.7 (AUT, between LLMs); kappa 84 vs 96 (TriviaQA). Not verified in paper text.
limits: Not blending tasks; creativity kappas not found.
agent_relevance: Gap 7: supports caution. Report kappa, not percent agreement, and check with a human-graded slice.
